concept.name: Actor Model Concurrency

relationships.description: Connects Actor Model Concurrency to python concurrency nogil in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: The Actor Model structures concurrent systems as isolated, share-nothing entities (actors) that encapsulate private state and communicate exclusively via asynchronous message passing into per-actor mailboxes (e.g., Erlang/OTP `GenServer`, Akka/Pekko, Microsoft Orleans).
spark.keyTakeaway: By processing one message at a time per actor and forbidding shared mutable memory, you eliminate mutexes and deadlocks—trading synchronous call convenience for mailbox backpressure and supervision trees.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional shared-memory threading breaks down under high concurrency: fine-grained locks cause deadlocks and cache-line ping-pong, while coarse locks serialize cores. The Actor Model powers telecom switches, WhatsApp, Discord's real-time guild servers, and stateful edge/IoT platforms because millions of lightweight actors can run across cores or cluster nodes with isolated failure domains.
whenToUse: High-cardinality stateful entities (chat rooms, game lobbies, IoT digital twins, order-book matching engines) where each entity serializes its own events.
Fault-tolerant services requiring hierarchical 'let it crash' isolation via supervision trees (Erlang/OTP, Akka) so one bad message doesn't take down the node.
Distributed cluster sharding where location transparency lets an actor migrate across nodes without changing caller code.
whenNotToUse: CPU-bound data-parallel workloads (matrix multiplication, video encoding, Monte Carlo) where SIMD, ForkJoin, or GPU kernels outperform message-passing overhead.
Simple stateless CRUD APIs backed by PostgreSQL/Redis where standard async/await request handlers are simpler to debug and scale.
Transactions requiring synchronous, multi-entity ACID joins across arbitrary actors—coordinating 2PC over actors reintroduces distributed locks.
keyPoints: Share-nothing isolation: an actor's internal state can only be read or mutated by that actor itself while processing a single message from its mailbox.
Three fundamental primitives on message receipt: send finite messages to known actors, spawn new actors, or designate the behavior for the next message.
Location transparency: sending a message (`pid ! msg` or `actorRef.tell(msg)`) uses the exact same syntax whether the target is in the same OS process or across the network.
Supervision trees decouple business logic from error recovery: parent supervisors restart, stop, or escalate crashed child actors using strategies like `one_for_one` or `one_for_all`.
Backpressure is mandatory: unbounded mailboxes turn slow consumers into JVM/BEAM out-of-memory crashes.

examples.title: Discord Real-Time Guild Fan-Out on BEAM
examples.scenario: A single Discord server (guild) with 500,000+ online members receives a burst of chat messages and presence updates.
examples.outcome: Each guild runs as an isolated Elixir/BEAM `GenServer` actor holding presence state in memory and fanning out messages asynchronously to member WebSocket processes; a crash in one guild restarts only that actor in milliseconds.

examples.title: IoT Fleet Digital Twins with Akka Cluster Sharding
examples.scenario: 2 million connected delivery vehicles stream GPS and battery telemetry every 5 seconds to a 20-node JVM cluster.
examples.outcome: Akka Cluster Sharding maps each `vehicle_id` to a single stateful `VehicleActor` across the cluster, deduplicating out-of-order packets and persisting state snapshots via Akka Persistence without external distributed locks.

tradeOffs.factor: Message-Passing Copy Overhead vs. Lock-Free Shared Memory
tradeOffs.pro: Zero data races, zero mutex contention, and predictable single-threaded reasoning inside each actor.
tradeOffs.con: Serialization and message-copying costs (especially across nodes) add latency compared to direct in-memory reads.

tradeOffs.pro: Bounded mailboxes cap heap usage and surface overload immediately via drop/dead-letter or backpressure signals.
tradeOffs.con: Requires explicit capacity sizing and reactive upstream throttling (e.g., Akka Streams or GenStage) to avoid silent message loss.

tradeOffs.pro: One actor per entity maximizes parallelism across CPU cores and isolates failures to a single entity.
tradeOffs.con: Too many tiny actors increase routing/mailbox memory overhead; too few create hot-spot bottlenecks.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Mailbox OOM
failureModes.description: A slow downstream actor (e.g., blocked on a DB write) receives 10,000 msgs/sec into an unbounded queue until the process OOM-kills.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure bounded mailboxes, use pull-based demand (Elixir `GenStage` / Akka Streams), or shed load at the edge.

failureModes.name: Head-of-Line Blocking in an Actor Turn
failureModes.description: An actor performs a blocking HTTP call or heavy CPU loop inside its message handler, starving all other messages in its mailbox and blocking scheduler threads.
failureModes.mitigation: Offload blocking I/O to a dedicated dispatcher/worker pool and pipe the result back as an asynchronous message.

failureModes.name: Supervisor Restart Storm
failureModes.description: A persistent poison-pill message or corrupt state causes a child actor to crash and restart infinitely, saturating CPU and logs.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `max_restarts` / `max_seconds` intensity limits on supervisors and route repeated failures to a dead-letter queue.

failureModes.name: Cluster Split-Brain (Dual Active Actors)
failureModes.description: A network partition splits an actor cluster; both halves assume the other is dead and spawn duplicate singleton/sharded actors for the same ID.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a Split-Brain Resolver (e.g., Pekko/Akka SBR with keep-majority or static-quorum) and fencing tokens on external DB writes.

commonMistakes: Using synchronous `ask` / `GenServer.call` everywhere, turning an asynchronous actor graph into a brittle RPC chain prone to cascading timeouts and deadlocks.
Sharing mutable objects (e.g., Java `HashMap` or `List`) inside messages instead of immutable records/structs, reintroducing data races.
Putting all system traffic through a single global 'manager' actor, creating a 1-core bottleneck.
Treating actor mailboxes as durable queues—mailboxes live in RAM and vanish on node crash unless backed by event sourcing or a broker.
Performing blocking JDBC/HTTP calls directly on the default actor dispatcher thread pool.

sections.content:
## The idea

Proposed by Carl Hewitt in 1973 and battle-tested in Ericsson's AXD301 ATM switches (99.9999999% uptime), the **Actor Model** treats the *actor*—not the thread or lock—as the fundamental unit of computation. An actor combines **private state**, a **behavior** (message handler), and a **mailbox** (FIFO queue).

Because no actor can inspect another actor's memory, concurrency hazards like torn reads and lock-order deadlocks disappear by construction. Scalability comes from running hundreds of thousands of lightweight actors (costing ~300 bytes–2 KB each in BEAM or virtual actors in Orleans) multiplexed onto a small pool of OS threads.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace an order-matching actor `OrderBook(BTC-USD)` in a clustered runtime:

1. **Ingress & Routing**: A WebSocket gateway receives `PlaceLimitOrder(user=42, side=BUY, price=64200, qty=0.5)` and sends it asynchronously (`tell`) to the shard coordinator for `BTC-USD`.
2. **Mailbox Enqueue**: The message lands in `OrderBook(BTC-USD)`'s bounded mailbox (capacity `10,000`). If the actor is idle, the scheduler dispatches it to a worker thread.
3. **Single-Threaded Turn**: `OrderBook` pops the message, matches it against its in-memory `asks` tree without acquiring any mutex, emits `TradeExecuted` events to a `SettlementActor`, and updates its private order book.
4. **Supervision on Fault**: If a malformed tick triggers an arithmetic exception, `OrderBook` crashes cleanly. Its parent `MarketSupervisor` catches the exit signal, restarts `OrderBook` from its last event-sourced snapshot, and notifies the client—leaving `ETH-USD` and `SOL-USD` completely untouched.

sections.content:
## Mailbox scheduling & supervision trees

Actor runtimes differ in how they schedule work and handle failure:

- **Preemptive vs. Cooperative Scheduling**: The Erlang BEAM VM uses **reduction-based preemptive scheduling** (~4,000 reductions per time slice), guaranteeing a runaway actor cannot starve other actors on the same core. JVM/CLR frameworks (Akka/Pekko, Orleans) rely on cooperative thread-pool dispatching, so a blocking call inside `onReceive` can starve sibling actors.
- **Supervision Strategies**: In OTP and Akka, supervisors never share state with children; they only observe exit signals. `one_for_one` restarts only the failed child, `one_for_all` restarts all siblings when their states are tightly coupled, and `rest_for_one` restarts only children started after the failed one.

## Actor runtimes & CSP comparison

| Runtime / Model | Language | Scheduling | Distributed Location Transparency | Supervision Trees | Best-Fit Workload |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Erlang / Elixir (BEAM)** | Erlang, Elixir | Preemptive (reductions) | Native (`node@host` PIDs) | Built-in OTP (`GenServer`) | Massive-connection messaging, telecom, soft real-time |
| **Apache Pekko / Akka** | Scala, Java | Cooperative (ForkJoin/Pinned) | Cluster Sharding + Artery | Built-in (`SupervisorStrategy`) | Low-latency JVM streaming, CQRS/ES digital twins |
| **Microsoft Orleans** | C# / .NET | Cooperative (Turn-based) | Virtual Actors (auto-activation) | Implicit (grain deactivation) | Game backends, high-scale stateful microservices |
| **Go (CSP)** | Go | Cooperative (M:N goroutines) | Manual (gRPC / NATS) | Manual (`errgroup` / panics) | Network proxies, CLI tools, stateless pipelines |

## Failure modes

1. **Mailbox Starvation & OOM**: Producers outpace a consumer actor, filling an unbounded queue until the JVM or BEAM crashes. *Fix*: Enforce bounded mailboxes with backpressure or drop-oldest/newest policies.
2. **Ask-Pattern Deadlocks**: Actor A calls `ask(B)` synchronously while B calls `ask(A)`—both block waiting for replies that sit behind the active turn in their own mailboxes. *Fix*: Default to `tell` (fire-and-forget) with correlation IDs.
3. **Hot-Actor Bottleneck**: Routing all tenant traffic through one `GlobalRouterActor` caps throughput at 1 CPU core. *Fix*: Shard by `tenant_id` or `entity_id`.
4. **Split-Brain Duplicate State**: Without a quorum-based Split-Brain Resolver, network partitions create two active instances of the same `actor_id`, corrupting external storage.

## Persistence, backpressure & cluster hygiene

Because actor state lives in RAM, production systems pair actors with **Event Sourcing** (appending events to Cassandra, PostgreSQL, or Kafka and taking periodic snapshots every $N$ events) so restarted actors reconstruct exact state.

For I/O boundaries, never let raw TCP sockets or Kafka consumers push unboundedly into actors; bridge them with demand-driven streams (`GenStage`, `Pekko Streams`) that propagate backpressure upstream when mailboxes reach high-water marks.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Ensure every message payload is strictly immutable (records, frozen dataclasses, or BEAM terms).
- [ ] Replace synchronous `ask` chains with asynchronous `tell` + correlation IDs wherever possible.
- [ ] Configure bounded mailboxes and dead-letter logging/metrics for every actor type.
- [ ] Isolate blocking database or HTTP calls onto dedicated I/O thread pools/dispatchers.
- [ ] Define explicit supervisor `max_restarts` / `max_seconds` budgets to prevent infinite restart loops.
- [ ] Enable a quorum-based Split-Brain Resolver before deploying Cluster Sharding in production.

interviewProblems.title: Actor Model Concurrency
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Actor Model Concurrency. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: The Actor Model structures concurrent systems as isolated, share-nothing entities (actors) that encapsulate private state and communicate exclusively via asynchronous message passing into per-actor mailboxes (e.g., Erlang/OTP `GenServer`, Akka/Pekko, Microsoft Orleans).

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Entity Actor applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Supervisor Tree.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Supervisor Tree experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Configure bounded mailboxes, use pull-based demand (Elixir `GenStage` / Akka Streams), or shed load at the edge.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: By processing one message at a time per actor and forbidding shared mutable memory, you eliminate mutexes and deadlocks—trading synchronous call convenience for mailbox backpressure and supervision trees.
Avoid trap: Using synchronous `ask` / `GenServer.call` everywhere, turning an asynchronous actor graph into a brittle RPC chain prone to cascading timeouts and deadlocks.
Avoid trap: Sharing mutable objects (e.g., Java `HashMap` or `List`) inside messages instead of immutable records/structs, reintroducing data races.
When to reach for it: High-cardinality stateful entities (chat rooms, game lobbies, IoT digital twins, order-book matching engines) where each entity serializes its own events.
When to reach for it: Fault-tolerant services requiring hierarchical 'let it crash' isolation via supervision trees (Erlang/OTP, Akka) so one bad message doesn't take down the node.

putItTogether.title: Putting Actor Model Concurrency Together
putItTogether.summary: By processing one message at a time per actor and forbidding shared mutable memory, you eliminate mutexes and deadlocks—trading synchronous call convenience for mailbox backpressure and supervision trees.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Actor Model Concurrency before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Each guild runs as an isolated Elixir/BEAM `GenServer` actor holding presence state in memory and fanning out messages asynchronously to member WebSocket processes; a crash in one guild restarts only that actor in milliseconds.
